# Original JPEGs: default-key OutGuess retrieval

## Why run this?

Some known Liber Primus images contain messages recovered with OutGuess. A newcomer may reasonably try the same operation on the other images. This experiment records what that particular retrieval does, including failures and unverified output, instead of assuming that every byte stream is a message or every failure means an empty image.

## Plan fixed before execution

The runner and plan were committed as `8bca8ba` before the first run. The scope is all 75 archived manuscript JPEGs, plus the 2014 opening image and the compasses cover. Every original-image SHA-256 is fixed in the plan. Thumbnails, screenshots and recompressed images are excluded.

Each image receives exactly one invocation of OutGuess with retrieval mode and the literal key `Default key`. The timeout is 20 seconds per invocation. Ten expected payload hashes serve as positive controls. All output files, exit codes and stderr diagnostics are retained, including empty output files and abnormal exits. A second complete run checks reproducibility; it is not counted as 77 additional independent discoveries.

## Result

A subsequent [guarded-build comparison](#/experiments/outguess-guard-sweep) retains these original inputs and key. It reproduces all output bytes while replacing the 41 abnormal exits with explicit iterator-guard diagnostics. The table below remains the result of the original baseline build.

| Observed category | Images | What it establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Known payload hash reproduced | 10 | Exact agreement with the archived extraction control |
| Nonempty output, exit code 0, no control | 21 | Unverified candidate bytes only |
| Retrieval rejected, exit code 1 | 5 | This retrieval did not succeed |
| Abnormal exit code 3221225620 | 41 | An unresolved failure of this tool/build on these inputs |
| Timeout | 0 | No invocation exceeded the declared time limit |

All 77 invocations were attempted. Ten controls matched. **The other 67 images are not established as free of hidden data.** The 21 candidate outputs are not authenticated messages, and the 41 abnormal exits prevent treating this as a clean image-wide negative result.

The repeated output length 58,152 occurs in 19 candidate records. It is a reported extraction length, not a discovered structure in the manuscript. The 21 candidate byte streams have distinct hashes. None contains the ASCII marker `-----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----`; that limited observation neither validates nor rules out a different encoding or payload type. No signature verification or interpretation of candidate contents was performed in this experiment.

## What the failure diagnostics tell us

The decimal process code `3221225620` is `0xC0000094`. Microsoft's [NTSTATUS reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-erref/596a1078-e883-4972-9bbc-49e60bebca55) assigns that value to `STATUS_INTEGER_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO`. This identifies the Windows status associated with the saved exits. It does not locate an instruction, identify a faulty source line, or prove whether the cause lies in upstream code, port changes, or another part of the build. No crash dump or debugger stack trace is available in this record.

A separate audit of the saved diagnostics finds the reported header `seed: 41408, len: 58152` on 65 images:

| Recorded outcome for that same header | Images | Output recorded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exit 0, unverified candidate bytes | 19 | 58,152 bytes each |
| Exit 1, retrieval rejected | 5 | Zero bytes |
| Exit 0xC0000094, abnormal termination | 41 | Zero bytes |

Thus the repeated header occurs with three different outcomes. The `len` diagnostic is the length reported by the tool, not confirmation that a valid payload of that size exists. Nor do the shared values establish intentional repeated content in the JPEGs. The logs alone do not explain their cause. Two other candidate outputs have different headers; the ten positive controls also use different headers.

The [diagnostic audit JSON](experiments/records/outguess-default-key/results/diagnostic-audit.json) preserves each image's reported seed, length, exit code and output size, tied to the original report's checksum. Reproduce this comparison from the experiment bundle without installing OutGuess or downloading the images:

```text
python experiments/records/outguess-default-key/audit_diagnostics.py
```

This command checks existing evidence; it is not another extraction trial. A useful debugging comparison would retain a positive control, a byte-producing case with the shared header, a rejected case, and an abnormal case. Keep the original files and key fixed, record the replacement executable and build settings, and collect a stack trace if it also terminates abnormally. A successful run with another build would still require checking the extracted bytes; it would not automatically validate them as a message.

## How to reproduce

Use Python 3.12.10 and a locally available OutGuess executable. See the [OutGuess guide](#/wiki/outguess) for original-file selection and the known-payload controls.

```
python experiments/records/outguess-default-key/run.py --outguess outguess --output my-outguess-run
python experiments/records/outguess-default-key/check.py
```

The first command creates a new directory, refuses to reuse an existing one, and records your executable's SHA-256. Replace `outguess` with its full executable path if necessary. The second command audits the saved experiment: every image hash, output hash, expected control and record count. It does not run OutGuess.

To repeat the exact saved run with the same executable:

```
python experiments/records/outguess-default-key/run.py --outguess outguess --check
```

This checks the tool hash, all statuses, diagnostics and every saved payload byte. Paths to temporary files are normalized in diagnostics; diagnostic content is otherwise retained. A different binary or platform may legitimately produce different diagnostics or error behavior. Run it into a new directory and compare it as a build variant rather than replacing this baseline.

## Tool and build limitation

The recorded binary was a local Windows port of upstream commit `24810e14327c2bbeedeaadd3e24491f2a4425c02`, built using MinGW-W64 GCC 16.1.0. Its SHA-256 is `b342b8b85d678d3b2ed26efab70fba2b3956725670be7149b89646868f0ebade`.

The existing build record describes use of the upstream allocation/read fallback instead of mmap, a compatibility byte-order helper, and binary-mode input on Windows. Matching the ten controls checks those particular extraction paths; it does not establish correct behavior on all other images. The 41 abnormal exits remain a substantial limitation. The executable is not included in the wiki downloads. A reader with a different build should preserve their new report as a comparison, not expect its executable hash to match.

## Retest and review

Codex ran the entire 77-image sweep twice on 20 October 2026. All return codes, normalized diagnostics and output bytes matched exactly. A separate saved-file audit checked all image and output hashes and the ten control comparisons. The original plan, key, timeout and image list did not change after the first run. The visual map was generated from the saved report; it does not run another extraction. Human review remains pending.

## What to test next

The most informative next variant is another documented OutGuess build on exactly the same files and key, focusing on whether the 41 abnormal exits persist. A new key is a different variable and should not be changed simultaneously if the purpose is to isolate build behavior. Other steganographic methods require their own clearly scoped experiment.

records.article:
# Original JPEGs: guarded OutGuess build comparison

## What this test asks

The original default-key sweep had 41 abnormal exits. Those failures leave an important question: did the retrieval reach an identifiable error condition, and would a more explicit check change the extracted bytes?

This variant uses a clean build with three diagnostic guards. A guard checks a condition before an operation that would otherwise be invalid and stops with an explanatory message. Here the checks concern the retrieval bit position, iterator capacity, and a zero iterator value used by a remainder operation. They are diagnostic changes, not a new decryption method.

The [original baseline](#/experiments/outguess-default-key) remains available with its unchanged results. Both records belong to the same experiment family.

## What stayed fixed

The inputs are all 75 manuscript JPEGs plus the 2014 opening image and compasses cover, in their original bytes. Image hashes, the literal key `Default key`, and the 20-second timeout match the baseline. No image was recompressed or edited. The ten known payload controls run first; a control failure would stop the sweep.

The scope and runner were committed as `40890c5` before execution. The earlier 13-case pilot helped establish the build procedure; those cases are included here and are not presented as unseen validation. This is one complete 77-image comparison, not a search over keys or build settings.

## What changed

The recorded executable was compiled afresh from upstream commit `24810e14327c2bbeedeaadd3e24491f2a4425c02`, with the documented Windows portability changes and explicit guard patches. All 54 C files were compiled; object files from the original build were not reused. The build specification records compiler identity, source hashes and commands.

The clean executable differs in hash from the archived pilot executable, although it reproduced all 13 pilot results exactly. The full comparison below uses the clean executable. This does not establish bit-for-bit reproducible compilation across toolchains.

## Results

| Baseline outcome | Guarded outcome | Images |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Successful exit | Same successful exit, diagnostic and bytes | 31 |
| Existing rejection | Same rejection, diagnostic and bytes | 5 |
| Abnormal exit | Explicit zero-iterator guard; unchanged empty output | 41 |

All ten positive controls match. The 31 successful exits consist of those ten controls and 21 unverified outputs. Every one of the 77 payload byte streams matches the baseline exactly; no new candidate output appeared.

All 41 changed cases report `Guard: iterator skipmod zero`, with their individual bit counts and offsets retained in the saved report. For example, LP1-14 reports `Guard: iterator skipmod zero at off=645437 bits=645682`. The guarded build checks this zero value before the iterator's remainder operation.

The [comparison graphic](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/comparison.svg) summarizes the counts. The [per-image comparison](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/comparison.json) and [complete diagnostics](experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/results/report.json) retain the underlying evidence.

## What the result means

The new build gives a specific diagnostic for all 41 previously abnormal cases. This is useful for investigating the implementation and for preventing those failures from being mistaken for clean negative results.

It does not authenticate the 21 candidate outputs. It does not prove any image lacks hidden data. Both executables share the same upstream source and Windows port, so this is not validation by an independent implementation or another platform. The guarded run is also not a captured stack trace from the original executable.

## Reproduce the saved comparison

Download this experiment's bundle and the original-images archive, then extract both into the same folder, preserving their paths. Follow the bundle's START-HERE file to verify the archive and required image hashes. From that folder run:

```text
python experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/compare.py --check
```

This needs Python and the supplied data, but does not execute OutGuess. It verifies the plan dependencies and image hashes, checks both sets of saved outputs, and compares bytes and diagnostics directly. It recomputes the saved comparison instead of trusting its reported equality flags.

To regenerate the chart after that audit:

```text
python experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/figure.py
```

## Repeat retrieval from a source build

Supply a clean checkout of the pinned upstream source and a compatible MinGW-W64 GCC toolchain. The included build script does not fetch or install these dependencies. Choose an output directory that does not yet exist:

```text
python experiments/records/outguess-guard-pilot/build.py --source /path/to/outguess-source --output /path/to/new-build
python experiments/records/outguess-guard-sweep/run.py --outguess /path/to/new-build/outguess.exe --output /path/to/new-results
```

The runner requires the recorded executable hash. If compilation produces a different hash, preserve its build report and define a separate comparison; do not overwrite the expected hash to make the check pass. The new-results directory must not already exist. The saved-evidence audit above checks the committed results, not this new directory. To rerun retrieval and compare directly with the committed results, use `run.py --outguess /path/to/new-build/outguess.exe --check`.

## Remaining work

Human review is pending. An independently documented platform or implementation would address a different uncertainty from the guard comparison. Candidate-payload analysis should be a separate bounded experiment, retaining all outputs and avoiding the assumption that process success implies a message.

records.article:
# How much do unresolved LP2 page joins change word-length counts?

The published LP2 word-length census joins adjacent pages when their archived text meets rune to rune. That rule yields **2,896 rune tokens**. If a separator is inserted at each of the **32 rune-to-rune page edges**, the same 12,956 runes yield **2,928 tokens**. This experiment measures how much the statistics depend on that parsing choice. It does not decide which edges actually split words in the manuscript.

![Side-by-side rune-token length counts for joined and separated page edges](experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/token-lengths.svg)

## Fixed comparison

Use the archived text for LP2-00–55 and the site's 29-rune alphabet. Remove slash and CR/LF row wraps, retain headings and other punctuation, and count rune runs with optional internal apostrophes. There are three prespecified readings: concatenate every page; insert a space at all 32 edges whose archived end and start are both runes; and insert a space at each such edge one at a time. No rune is changed or omitted. The [boundary inventory](#/wiki/transcription-checking?section=page-joins) supplies the distinction between a rune-to-rune candidate and a verified word join.

| Measure | All edges joined | All 32 candidates separated |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Rune tokens | 2,896 | 2,928 |
| One-rune tokens | 83 | 99 |
| Two-rune tokens | 448 | 465 |
| Three-rune tokens | 720 | 726 |
| Tokens at least 10 runes long | 109 | 104 |
| Maximum token length | 14 | 14 |
| 11–11–10 length windows | 1 | 1 |

All 32 individual splits add exactly one token under this tokenizer. Five individual edges—LP2-21/22, 24/25, 42/43, 46/47 and 52/53—each reduce the number of tokens at least 10 runes long by one. The [machine-readable result](experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/results.json) lists every edge separately. The LP2-21 11–11–10 observation survives both endpoint policies, but this says nothing about its chance frequency or interpretation.

These endpoints are sensitivity cases, not manuscript corrections. A real reading could join some edges and split others. The source text can also omit a mark, and rune-to-rune edges can cross section boundaries. Word counts, repeated-token counts and word-reset cipher inputs depend on the boundary rule; rune frequencies and whole-stream IoC do not, because both versions contain the identical ordered runes. The reported 2,896 tokens are a transparent parsing convention, not 2,896 established words.

## Reproduce and extend

With Python 3 and no packages, run `python experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/run.py --check` and `python experiments/records/page-join-sensitivity/check.py` from the repository root or the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/page-join-sensitivity.zip). The first command checks the source hashes, complete report and figure. The second uses an independent character scanner to verify the 32 candidate edges, the two histograms, every one-edge token count, and the invariant 12,956-rune total. The plan fixes the inputs and three comparisons before interpreting them.

The next useful refinement is to record image-reviewed separators at particular edges and rerun the same script with those decisions frozen. Until then, a word-based cipher claim should specify its page-edge policy and show whether its result survives plausible changes at the relevant edges. See the [word-length guide](#/wiki/word-lengths) for the counting rules and complete token ledger.

## What changed from the baseline

The [full-corpus comparison](#/experiments/parallel-languages) used 1,012 evaluation sentences per language. Here we divide that evaluation split into **eight consecutive, disjoint blocks** and compare shorter passages. Each block contains the same sentence IDs in all eight languages. No sentences were chosen because their statistics looked promising.

The first four blocks contain 127 sentences each, and the last four contain 126. Exact one-based sentence ranges are recorded in the results. The plan was committed before block scoring; its dependency hash was then refreshed for a chart-only change in the baseline, before scoring began. The tokenization and distance definitions are unchanged.

## Results

**English is the closest of the eight language profiles to the pooled manuscript in all eight blocks, in each of the three representations.** This supports the stability of that relative ranking across these shorter passages. It does not identify the plaintext language.

Using letter units, the block sizes and manuscript distances are:

| Language | Tokens per block, range | Word-length distance, range |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| English | 2,613–3,002 | 0.0710–0.1035 |
| Finnish | 1,927–2,105 | 0.3726–0.4316 |
| French | 3,047–3,318 | 0.1731–0.2079 |
| German | 2,623–2,927 | 0.1696–0.1961 |
| Italian | 2,880–3,181 | 0.2274–0.2467 |
| Portuguese | 2,818–3,147 | 0.2007–0.2300 |
| Spanish | 3,106–3,467 | 0.2091–0.2402 |
| Welsh | 2,884–3,206 | 0.1416–0.1940 |

The target has 2,896 rune tokens. These are smaller aligned passages, not exactly size-matched samples: their token counts range from **1,927 to 3,467**. Translating the same content changes word counts. Keeping the same sentence ranges preserves the content control; truncating every language at exactly 2,896 words would no longer compare exactly the same passages. This design documents that tradeoff rather than hiding it.

## Does the statistic recognize known languages at this scale?

For each block, we compare its word-length histogram against all eight full development-language histograms. The closest development profile is the corresponding language in **64 of 64 decisions**, separately for letter units, accent-folded letters, and GP grouping. The raw report includes every distance and the full confusion matrices, including zeros.

That is a control on these eight translated languages within FLORES. It is not a success rate for cipher language identification. The corpus shares translation practices and source genre; the manuscript does not. The three representations also reuse the same text and are not independent replications.

## Bounds and limitations

- All 1,012 evaluation sentences are used once per language, with no overlap between blocks. Development text is used only for the reference profiles.
- A source article can cross a block boundary. Blocks are therefore not independent draws, and the 64 decisions are not treated as independent trials. No binomial accuracy interval or language posterior is calculated.
- The manuscript remains pooled LP2-00–55, with headings and the baseline boundary convention. This does not test each section separately.
- Word-length comparison requires preserved boundaries and one ciphertext rune per counted plaintext unit. GP grouping remains an orthographic sensitivity, not a validated phonetic transcription.
- No genre-matched corpus or known decoded LP control is included in this variant. The separate [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) now covers the nine documented LP sections. A genre-matched corpus remains open.

## Reproduce

The experiment download includes the aligned corpus, token ledger, baseline helper, independent tokenizer, frozen plan and result ledger. Python 3 standard library only; no network, API or model is used.

```sh
python experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/run.py --check
python experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/check.py
```

The first command verifies input hashes and recomputes the full report. The second independently reconstructs all 192 block profiles with a regex tokenizer and exact rational total-variation distances, checks all nearest-reference decisions, and verifies that the block ranges cover the evaluation sentences exactly once. Human review is pending.

[Results and confusion matrices](experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/results.json) · [Frozen plan](experiments/records/parallel-language-blocks/plan.json) · [Baseline distributions and source attribution](#/experiments/parallel-languages)

FLORES source text and this derived account are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0. See the source attribution included with the baseline files.

## What this comparison tells us

**English is closest by word lengths among these eight languages.** The ordering of other close candidates changes when a fixed GP-style grouping is applied to all eight. This is a comparison of statistical shapes under stated assumptions. It does not identify the plaintext or decipher a word.

The experiment uses translations of the **same 997 development sentences and 1,012 evaluation sentences** from FLORES-200. The languages were fixed before scoring: English, Welsh, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Finnish. They give a manageable Latin-script comparison without adding a transliteration model for other scripts. They are not a shortlist inferred from the manuscript, and the ranking is not a search across all languages.

The plan and source files were committed in `738a812` before any scores were calculated. It is a predeclared comparison within this project, not an external preregistration. Human review is pending.

## Word-length results

The distance is **total variation** between word-length distributions: half the sum of their absolute frequency differences. Zero means identical distributions; one means no overlap. We count lengths 1 through 15 separately and put longer words in a final 16+ bin. A value of 0.084 is a distance, not an 8.4% chance of anything.

| Language | Letters | GP grouping sensitivity |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| English | 0.0840 | 0.1148 |
| Welsh | 0.1721 | 0.1731 |
| German | 0.1757 | 0.1708 |
| French | 0.1827 | 0.1759 |
| Portuguese | 0.2131 | 0.2058 |
| Spanish | 0.2240 | 0.2127 |
| Italian | 0.2359 | 0.2311 |
| Finnish | 0.4022 | 0.3927 |

[Open the comparison chart](experiments/records/parallel-languages/comparison.svg). The chart shows the same results with article-resampling ranges. The JSON also contains the accent-folded letter comparison, which keeps the same language order.

The ordering depends on the counting convention. A language ranking is conditional on both the corpus and the assumed relationship between plaintext units and ciphertext runes. The full table keeps every tested candidate visible.

## Why the rankings differ

The manuscript has a pronounced peak at length three: **24.86% of its tokens contain three runes**. The language profiles differ in how much mass they place at each length. The distribution chart shows the manuscript first, followed by all eight languages alphabetically, using identical scales and the same styling for every language.

The first-place result still has a visible mismatch: English has 19.07% three-letter words, below the manuscript's three-rune share. A ranking measures relative closeness among the tested profiles; it does not establish that the nearest profile is a good explanation of the ciphertext.

[Open all nine distribution panels](experiments/records/parallel-languages/distributions.svg). Lengths 9 and above are combined only for display; scoring retains the original 16 bins. Every full distribution is also available in the results JSON.

## The assumptions that make lengths useful

This comparison requires manuscript word boundaries to preserve plaintext word boundaries, and one counted plaintext unit to correspond to one ciphertext rune. A position-dependent substitution can preserve lengths even when letter frequencies change. Inserted nulls, deleted symbols, word splitting, different spacing, or units representing syllables can break the comparison.

The manuscript target is the existing [rune-token ledger](exports/unsolved-word-tokens.json): **2,896 tokens and 12,956 runes from LP2-00–55**, including headings. Line wraps and slash wraps are removed; tokens can continue across page boundaries. Internal apostrophes count zero, and decimal labels are excluded. See [word lengths](#/wiki/word-lengths) for the exact boundary convention and its historical alternatives. Pooling the pages assumes their aggregate is meaningful; it does not establish that every section has one language or cipher.

For FLORES, letters are lowercased and normalized to NFC. Alphabetic runs are words; internal straight or curly apostrophes are removed without splitting the word. Hyphens and other nonletters separate words. Numbers contribute no letters. Each sentence is tokenized independently. This is an explicit mechanical convention, not a linguist's definition of a word. The comparison retains every aligned sentence; it does not truncate each language to a different passage to equalize word totals.

The GP sensitivity folds combining accents and greedily groups ING, TH, EO, NG, OE, AE, IA, IO and EA, longest first. ING/NG, IO/IA, K/C and Z/S share symbols. Other letters remain. **This is not a validated translation into Gematria Primus.** Pronunciation, ambiguous segmentation and unsupported letters remain unresolved. A supplementary mechanical Welsh-digraph calculation is retained in the raw data as a representation check, not as a separate candidate category or a preferred model. It groups CH, DD, FF, NG, LL, PH, RH and TH and gives a length distance of 0.1466; it does not resolve morphological parsing. The raw-letter and GP profiles can contain more than 29 distinct symbols, so they cannot be literal bijective mappings into a 29-rune alphabet as written. This inventory mismatch is reported in the downloadable results rather than silently repaired by deleting rare letters.

## Repetition gives a different test

IoC is the probability that two different sampled positions contain the same symbol. Adjacent repetition here counts equal neighbors **within words only**. Both require stronger assumptions than lengths: equality must survive a fixed one-to-one substitution. They are not preserved by a general polyalphabetic cipher.

| Text, using letter units | IoC | Equal adjacent pairs |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Unsolved rune target | 0.03448 | 0.63% |
| English | 0.06597 | 2.42% |
| Welsh | 0.06387 | 5.74% |
| German | 0.07344 | 2.33% |
| French | 0.06912 | 2.42% |
| Portuguese | 0.07072 | 1.00% |
| Spanish | 0.07111 | 0.77% |
| Italian | 0.07305 | 4.57% |
| Finnish | 0.07282 | 9.31% |

The language profiles have letter IoCs between **0.06387 and 0.07344**, far from the target's **0.03448**. None of these profiles supplies a close single-substitution explanation of the pooled manuscript. The GP sensitivity does not remove that discrepancy. Spanish is closest on the adjacent-repeat measure, yet has a much poorer word-length match. These conflicting rankings are why we do not blend the measures into an unexplained “language likelihood.”

This does not eliminate Welsh, English or any other language under a different cipher. It weakens the proposed fixed-substitution comparison under these text and unit conventions. See [cipher invariants](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) for what different transformations preserve.

## Controls and sampling sensitivity

Each development-language word-length profile was compared with each evaluation-language profile. The nearest development profile identified the corresponding evaluation language **8 out of 8 times in each of the three representations**. That is a useful check that this dataset and statistic can distinguish the chosen languages at this sample size. It is not 100% accuracy on unknown manuscripts: there are only eight whole-document controls, drawn from the same benchmark, and they are much longer than the target.

For the error bars we resample the **281 source-article URL groups** in the evaluation split, with replacement, 200 times using seed 3301. All sentences from a sampled article are kept. The same article draw is used for all eight languages, preserving the matched-content comparison and avoiding treating every sentence as independent. English has the smallest length distance in all 200 draws in all three representations. This is stability to this corpus resampling—not a 100% probability that the manuscript is English. The target transcription is held fixed; these intervals omit uncertainty about its boundaries, genre and cipher.

FLORES contains translated web material. It controls subject matter across languages, but not the difference between that material and Liber Primus's philosophical style, historical spelling or possible nonstandard prose. Translation practices can also affect lengths. A separately fixed, genre-matched parallel corpus remains a follow-up. The [exact-token control](#/experiments/target-sized-languages) now checks complete 2,896-token samples: all reference samples identify their own language profile, but every manuscript-to-profile distance exceeds the corresponding observed control range. Those ranges are descriptive, not confidence limits or rejection thresholds. The [known-LP reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) is now complete as a computational comparison, with human review pending. A separate [shorter aligned-block variant](#/experiments/parallel-language-blocks) now checks eight disjoint evaluation blocks per language; it preserves matching sentences rather than enforcing exactly equal word counts.

## Reproduce it

Download this experiment's bundle. It includes the source translations, source-article metadata, plan, token ledger, scripts, result JSON and chart. No API, account, model download or network request is needed to rerun the analysis; Python 3's standard library is enough.

```sh
python experiments/records/parallel-languages/run.py --check
python experiments/records/parallel-languages/check.py
python experiments/records/parallel-languages/distribution_figure.py --check
```

The first command verifies input hashes, recomputes the comparisons and the 200 resamples, and checks the saved report and chart. Without `--check`, it writes those two outputs. The second uses a separate regex tokenizer and integer-count formulas to verify the 24 language profiles, additional digraph sensitivity, manuscript profile, IoC, repeated neighbors, distances and ordering. It does not independently reimplement the bootstrap. The final command checks that the distribution chart matches the saved counts; it does not perform another experiment. The ledger itself has a separate [transcription/word-length reproduction](#/wiki/word-lengths).

[Raw results](experiments/records/parallel-languages/results.json) · [Frozen plan](experiments/records/parallel-languages/plan.json) · [Source attribution](experiments/records/parallel-languages/SOURCE.txt)

## Sources and reuse

- [FLORES-200 documentation](https://github.com/facebookresearch/flores/blob/main/flores200/README.md): aligned translation benchmark and language list.
- [Original archive](https://dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/nllb/flores200_dataset.tar.gz): exact extracted translation and metadata files; archive and extracted-file hashes are recorded in the plan.
- [Dataset card and license](https://huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/flores): Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International. Source translations are redistributed unchanged. This derived analysis and its article are also offered under CC BY-SA 4.0.

## Check against known LP readings

The [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) now tests all nine established reading sections and their pool. The pool ranks closest to English, while some individual sections do not. It also documents how LP2-56's embedded hash distorts an unfiltered letter-token count. This supplies a manuscript-specific caution beyond the within-FLORES controls.

records.article:
# Can each rune label a divisor of its position?

**Not with consecutive positions, under the rule tested here.** Every nonempty rune page in LP2-00–55 contains repeated occurrences whose spacing makes a fixed divisor greater than one impossible, regardless of where counting starts. This is a fresh reproduction of the supplied closure archive's C11 claim, not an original discovery.

## Define the rule before testing it

Let i be a zero-based rune position within a page. Choose an integer origin N and a fixed stride s. Assign each rune r an integer divisor q[r] greater than one, then require:

```text
q[r] divides N + s*i whenever position i contains r
```

The same rune must keep the same divisor throughout that page. Divisors need not be prime, distinct, or equal to Gematria Primus values. Allowing all integers greater than one makes this test more permissive than an assignment restricted to primes. Each page may use its own origin, stride and assignment.

This is a necessary condition for a direct smallest-factor or largest-factor labeling proposal. It does not test prime-derived keys combined with plaintext or an arbitrary operation that merely uses prime numbers.

## Why the origin cancels

If q divides both N+s*i and N+s*j, it divides their difference s*(j−i). The unknown N disappears. For several occurrences, q must therefore divide the stride multiplied by the gcd of the position gaps.

For unit stride, a gap gcd of 1 would require q to divide 1. That contradicts q > 1. Running the page backwards changes the origin and stride sign, not this obstruction.

A rune appearing only once has no gap constraint. Two occurrences with gap 1 already suffice; otherwise several gaps may be needed. The report records every occurrence and, where available, a three-occurrence gcd-one witness. It uses gcd 0 for an empty set of gaps; that means no restriction from this particular test, not impossibility.

## A witness on LP2-00

F occurs at zero-based rune positions **7, 17 and 58**. Thus a fixed divisor must divide both 10 and 51 under unit stride. Their gcd is 1. This single repeated rune already rules out the model on that page; the report records the other rune labels as well.

These are positions in the filtered rune stream, including the heading. They are not image coordinates, Latin-letter offsets or positions that count punctuation.

## What the full retest covers

The program reads all 56 archived text files LP2-00–55, retains alphabet runes and headings, and starts each page independently. All **55 nonempty streams** have at least one gcd-one rune. LP2-50 has no alphabet runes in this transcription and is skipped; its alphanumeric grid is not converted into runes.

Every page therefore excludes both forward and reverse unit-stride constructions, even when the origin and arbitrary integer divisor labels are chosen independently for that page. This is an exact contradiction under the stated model, not a low probability or a finite search over origins.

## Why arbitrary strides remain different

With a gcd-one witness, the general condition is **q divides s**. It excludes a stride coprime to that rune's divisor. It does not exclude every nonunit stride.

For a concrete counterexample, set N=2, s=2 and q[r]=2 for every rune. Every position N+s*i is even, so every recorded rune passes the divisibility condition on every page. This construction assigns the same divisor to different runes, which the tested necessary condition permits. It supplies no decoding rule and does not identify which rune to emit at a position.

If a proposal requires distinct labels, literal GP primes, or a deterministic factor-selection rule, those extra requirements need separate analysis. The counterexample refutes the broader claim that this divisibility condition alone excludes all strides; it is not a successful cipher.

## Reproduce and independently check

Download the experiment ZIP and keep its folders intact. Python 3's standard library is sufficient; no network, AI calls or additional packages are needed.

```text
python experiments/records/position-divisor-labels/run.py --check
python experiments/records/position-divisor-labels/check.py
```

The first program uses distances from each rune's first occurrence. The independent checker reads page JSON and computes the gcd of all pairwise occurrence distances. It also verifies every displayed triple, the stride-two counterexample on all 55 pages, a valid unit-stride control, and 450 small synthetic origin/stride cases.

Both text sources share archival ancestry: agreement is a computation check, not an independent manuscript transcription review. The earlier archive cites a Lean proof; this package provides elementary reasoning and fresh integer checks, without claiming that the Lean development was rerun.

## Limits and reopening conditions

Changing which characters advance the clock, resetting within a page, changing a rune's divisor over time, selecting an irregular sequence of integers, or transforming the factor labels changes the model. Such proposals are not ruled out here. A transcription correction also requires a new run. This result belongs alongside other bounded exclusions, not under a heading claiming that prime-based ciphers are impossible.

# Why the reported 53-digit reverse-add result is a palindrome

## The precise claim

A [prior LP2-15 discussion](#/wiki/reported-attempts?section=lp2-15-prime-distance-palindromes) reports distances from word-level GP sums to nearby primes. After concatenating a selected sequence of those distances, the author added the 53-character decimal string to its reversal and obtained a 53-digit palindrome. The thread corrected an earlier 46-digit claim to 53 digits.

This experiment checks **that arithmetic and one conditional baseline**. It does not reconstruct the word-to-distance sequence from the manuscript, certify the zero-based grouping, or test a decipherment rule. The exact source excerpt is identified in the [structured intake](data/reported-attempts.json) by SHA-256. The decimal string and claimed sum are copied into `plan.json`, so the arithmetic replay needs no external account or chat export.

## Input and result

```text
  02311171210211215142515300303126131002122052400021111
+ 11112000425022120013162130300351524151211201217111320
= 13423171635233335155677430603477655153333253617132431
```

The addition is correct and the result reads identically in either direction. The first operand's leading zero is retained when constructing the reversal; as an integer it has no value, but dropping it before reversing would define a different operation.

The more informative fact is that **every paired digit sum is at most 7**. No column carries. If a decimal string has digits `d[0] ... d[n−1]`, adding it to its reversal pairs `d[i]` with `d[n−1−i]`. These pair sums are necessarily mirror-symmetric. Whenever all are below ten, and the outer pair is nonzero, the decimal result must be a palindrome. The reported example meets both conditions. Its palindromicity follows from this elementary rule; it does not require a cipher mechanism.

![Fifty-three source-derived paired sums mirror around the center and all remain below the decimal carry line of ten.](experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/paired-sums.svg)

## A matched-digit control

The plan fixes 100,000 pseudorandom shuffles of the **same 53 characters**, with Python's `random.Random(3301)` and no restrictions on a leading zero in the shuffled string. Each shuffled string is reversed and added as an integer exactly as above. **50,442 of 100,000** shuffles yield palindromes. In this run, exactly the same 50,442 satisfy the no-carry condition with a nonzero outer pair.

This is a conditional, descriptive control: it preserves the selected digit multiset but not any GP word order. It is not a p-value for the full search that produced the string. That search could choose pages, word boundaries, nearest-prime ties, zero separators, and which examples to present. A null model for the whole idea must include those choices. Randomly shuffling uniform decimal digits would be a different and less relevant comparison, because the reported distances concentrate at small digits (11 zeroes, 18 ones, 11 twos).

## Reproduce

Extract the [experiment bundle](downloads/experiments/prime-distance-reverse-add.zip) with folders intact, then run from its root:

```text
python experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/run.py --check
python experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/check.py
python experiments/records/prime-distance-reverse-add/plot.py
```

The first command recomputes the arithmetic and all 100,000 fixed shuffles. The independent checker verifies the 53 column sums, their symmetry, the no-carry proof condition, and the saved control's internal consistency. The plotter regenerates the SVG from `results.json`. All use the Python standard library. `plan.json` specifies the original digits, seed, trial count and post-selection scope; `results.json` preserves the full paired-sum list and control counts.

## What remains open

The decimal result is reproducible, but the **source-to-digits derivation** is not yet. An end-to-end replay must pin the LP2-15/16 transcription, GP alphabet, word and section boundaries, nearest-prime tie rule, and treatment of zeros and leading zeros. It should enumerate every eligible section and grouping before selecting a notable output, then apply the identical search to matched controls. A rare result under that complete search would be more informative than a rare-looking decimal string chosen after several transformations.

This computational audit was run and checked by Codex on 2026-10-22. Human review of the source grouping and the mathematical interpretation is pending.

records.article:
## Why test a whole search?

A candidate can look better simply because we tried more keys. Comparing that winner with one randomly chosen wrong key ignores the selection that produced it. This experiment repeats an entire declared search on null ciphertexts, retaining its best score each time.

The best null scores rise as the nested dictionary grows from one to 256 keys, but none crosses the fixed −5.5 acceptance threshold in this grid. Searches of positive ciphertext also fail that threshold when the true key is absent. Appending the true key makes every positive control recover exactly and pass. These outcomes describe this finite search; they are not a guarantee against false positives in larger or different searches.

## Three conditions, kept separate

| Condition | Ciphertext | Keys searched | What it checks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Null | Reproducible uniform pseudorandom rune indices | A declared wrong-key dictionary | The best score selected from the whole dictionary under this null generator. |
| Positive, key absent | A known rune prefix encrypted by addition modulo 29 | The same dictionary, excluding its true seed | What a search reports when its intended answer is outside its bounds. |
| Positive, key included | The same positive ciphertext | That dictionary plus its true key | Whether inclusion recovers the known answer and whether it wins the scoring comparison. |

The included condition has **one more candidate** than the stated wrong-key budget. At budget 256 it compares 257 candidates. Its known key is not secretly inserted into the other conditions, and its exact-recovery check is separate from score acceptance.

## Inputs and bounds

All nine known-reading traces contribute their first 240 output rune indices, or their full length when shorter. Their lengths range from 85 to 240 runes. These are existing trace outputs, not edited English converted back into runes. No section is removed because of a poor score or unusual content.

For each section, 32 replicates generate a null ciphertext and a positive ciphertext of that section's length. Each null uses a fresh, recorded Python pseudorandom-generator seed and uniform draws from indices 0–28. Each positive uses the known prefix and a recorded derived key. The paired controls share length and search settings; they do not share ciphertext.

The candidate keys use SHA-256 over a fixed ASCII seed label and a four-byte big-endian counter, with digest bytes reduced modulo 29. Because 256 is not divisible by 29, this reduction is biased. It is an explicit fixture, not a uniform-pad claim. Candidate seeds are 0–255; positive seeds are 100000–100031 and therefore absent from that dictionary.

For every candidate, subtract its key from the ciphertext modulo 29, transliterate with the canonical rune labels, and average the English quadgram log scores. The unseen-quadgram count is 0.01 and the threshold is −5.5, inherited unchanged from the [scorer controls](#/experiments/english-scorer-controls). There are no offsets, alternate signs, skip rules or word-boundary adjustments.

## Nested search budgets

Every search retains all 256 individual candidate scores and examines dictionary prefixes of 1, 4, 16, 64 and 256 keys. A larger budget contains every candidate in the smaller one. Its maximum therefore cannot decrease. Ties use the smallest seed ID, including when comparing an appended true key.

The figures preserve all nine source sections. At each budget, a dot is the median of the 32 best scores and the vertical line is their full observed range. Neither is a confidence interval. All panels share a score scale. The positive included condition has a constant score within a section because exact decryption returns the same known rune prefix despite different encryption keys.

| Wrong-key budget | Null accepted | Positive accepted, true key absent | Positive exact and accepted, true key included |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (2 candidates) |
| 4 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (5 candidates) |
| 16 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (17 candidates) |
| 64 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (65 candidates) |
| 256 | 0/288 | 0/288 | 288/288 (257 candidates) |

These are counts over the fixed grid, not independent-trial accuracy estimates. The full CSV keeps each section separate across all 135 section/budget/condition combinations. The JSON retains all 147,456 wrong-key scores, 288 true-key controls, ciphertexts, seeds, candidate hashes and search winners.

## What a zero count means

We observed no threshold exceedances among these null searches. That does not prove the threshold is safe for a million-key search, a beam decoder, several language models, or repeated human choices about which output to keep. Such procedures offer different opportunities to find a high-scoring candidate and need their own controls.

The sections share source material, the dictionary is reused, and budgets are nested. Repetition does not turn this into 288 independent texts drawn from all possible plaintext. The null generator is also a chosen model, not an established description of the manuscript. We do not estimate a probability that a manuscript candidate is correct, pool the scores into an anomaly verdict, or infer a cipher family.

The [decoder alignment controls](#/experiments/decoder-skip-controls) demonstrate a complementary limitation: even a correct key can fail under an unsuitable decoder, and an incorrect rune sequence can pass a language score. Here the positive controls validate only ordinary modular addition and this declared dictionary search.

## Reproduce and inspect

Extract the experiment ZIP with its folder structure intact. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient; there are no network requests, API calls or paid services.

```text
python experiments/records/search-maximum-controls/run.py --check
python scripts/check_search_maximum_controls.py experiments/records/search-maximum-controls/results.json --receipt my-search-audit.json
python experiments/records/search-maximum-controls/plot.py
```

The independent checker imports no producer functions. It rebuilds the source prefixes, null ciphertexts and derived keys, checks every candidate hash, recalculates scores using counted quadgrams, and reconstructs every winner and tie decision. It also checks monotonic maxima and the additional candidate count when the true key is appended. All 288 paired searches passed; human review remains pending.

The practical lesson is to compare a selected result with controls that undergo the same selection. See [search space and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) and [null models](#/wiki/null-models). A different dictionary, decoder, scoring rule or adaptive workflow should be a documented variant, with the complete search repeated in its controls.

records.article:
# Does matching the opening text identify a seed?

A short readable opening can have several explanations. This experiment plants a known 95-rune passage under two fixed keystream generators, searches a finite seed dictionary, and asks whether seeds that reproduce the opening also predict the remaining text. No candidate is selected by looking at that remaining text.

A **crib** is an assumed exact plaintext sequence at an exact position. Here the crib is supplied as part of the control. It is not guessed from the ciphertext or inferred from a language score. The **withheld suffix** is everything after the crib: the part reserved for checking a prediction.

With two crib runes, every tested search retains several seeds. Only the true generating pairs recover the complete passage. At four or more crib runes, those generating pairs are the only survivors in the searches that include them; the other controls retain none. This is a result for these fixtures and dictionaries, not a general four-rune requirement.

## What is searched?

The plaintext is the 95 output rune indices from the known reading of LP2-57. New ciphertexts are generated from it. This is not a new attempt to decrypt the original LP2-57 image, and it supplies no claim about the unsolved pages.

The two generators use SHA-256 and SHA-512. Each hashes the ASCII domain separator `liberpedia-seed-control:v1:`, followed by a four-byte unsigned big-endian seed and a four-byte unsigned big-endian counter starting at zero. Digest bytes of 232 or greater are discarded; the remaining bytes are reduced modulo 29. Digests are concatenated until 95 indices are available. There are no skips, offsets, resets or alternate signs.

Each generator plants seeds 17, 4095 and 4096. Each search tests seeds **0 through 4095**, inclusive, under one generator. Seed 4096 is deliberately absent from both search dictionaries even though it is a valid generator input. Thus an unsuccessful search can simply mean the needed seed is outside its bounds.

Encryption is `cipher[i] = (plain[i] + key[i]) mod 29`. A seed survives when it reproduces every assumed crib rune at the start. Every survivor is retained; there is no English score, best-candidate ranking or phrase selection. Its complete decoded sequence is then compared with the known plaintext, keeping full-passage equality and withheld-suffix equality separate.

## Results

The figure reports the range of candidate counts across the searches in each control group. These ranges are not confidence intervals. The incorrect-crib group changes only the first rune by adding one modulo 29, leaving the rest of the assumed opening unchanged. It includes both matching and mismatched search generators.

| Control | Searches per crib length | Survivors with 2 crib runes | Survivors with 4, 8, 16 or 32 crib runes |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| Correct crib; generating pair included | 4 | 4, 6, 11, 8 | Exactly 1 per search |
| Correct crib; matching generator but seed outside range | 2 | 5, 4 | 0 |
| Correct crib; wrong generator | 6 | 8, 5, 10, 6, 8, 2 | 0 |
| Incorrect first crib rune | 12 | 6, 5, 2, 7, 4, 3, 8, 6, 7, 4, 4, 6 | 0 |

At length two, the four included-pair searches contain 29 survivors in total. Four are the true generating pairs; the other 25 fail to predict the complete 93-rune withheld suffix. All survivors in the other three control groups also fail that complete suffix test. They may agree with individual withheld runes, which is why the full report preserves both exact equality and the number of correct positions.

For all longer tested cribs, each included-pair search retains exactly the true seed, which recovers all 95 runes. An incorrect first crib rune prevents full-passage equality by construction; the independently evaluated suffix test is a separate check.

The complete summary retains all **120 cells**, including zero-survivor cases. The full JSON also stores every searched keystream, every planted ciphertext and every surviving candidate's decoded sequence. A generating-pair identity and an exact finite-stream match are conceptually different; no alternative pair recovers the whole passage in these controls.

## What an empty search establishes

An empty result excludes only the tested generator/seed pairs under the exact crib and alignment. It does not exclude seeds outside the dictionary, other generators, another seed encoding, a different crib, an unknown offset or a different cipher mechanism. The two omitted-seed fixtures demonstrate this directly: their ciphertexts are generated by a tested generator, yet the bounded correct-crib searches retain no seed once the crib reaches four runes.

These cells reuse one plaintext and fixed dictionaries. They are dependent controls, not independent samples from a population of ciphers. Short prefixes can match accidentally; no probability that an LP proposal is correct follows from these counts. Random-looking ciphertext also does not establish an independent one-time pad.

## Reproduce and inspect

Extract this experiment's ZIP with folders intact, or use the repository. Python 3 and its standard library are sufficient; no additional corpus, original-image download, API or model is needed.

```sh
python experiments/records/seed-crib-controls/run.py --check
```

The command reconstructs the result, independently checks every stream and survivor, and compares the complete summary and figure. Use `--output seed-replay` instead to retain newly generated reports in a new directory. The plot can also be regenerated with `python experiments/records/seed-crib-controls/plot.py`.

The protocol was committed before candidate generation. The checker imports no producer code: it separately packs seed/counter bytes, uses division to implement rejection conversion and checks compatibility by directly encrypting the assumed crib. Both implementations share Python's hash primitives. Boundary and exhaustive toy controls test byte order, the 231/232 cutoff and the difference between prefix, suffix and whole-text agreement. Human review remains pending.

## Related explanations

Read [search spaces and bounds](#/wiki/search-space) for interpreting an empty search, [one-time pads and short seeds](#/wiki/one-time-pad) for the identification limits, and [search-maximum controls](#/experiments/search-maximum-controls) for the different problem of selecting the highest language score.

records.article:
# Selected phrase and MYRMELEONTIDAE word sums

This variant changes the baseline's candidate list to five supplied words: PROVE, WORTHIER, FIND, TRUTHS and MYRMELEONTIDAE. The first four were proposed against totals 131, 151, 151 and 131; the last against 809. It checks those selected matches without claiming that the resulting phrase or name is recovered plaintext.

## What changes from the baseline?

The [baseline word-sum audit](#/experiments/mixed-square-word-sums) tests sixteen other supplied word-and-total pairs, including FIND. This variant retains the same 29-label alphabet, V-to-U normalization, exhaustive segmentation procedure and prime-value summation. Only the candidate list and proposed targets change. FIND is intentionally retained as a shared check.

The candidate list was fixed before enumeration, but the supplied words were already selected for their claimed numerical matches. This is an exploratory audit, not an unbiased measure of how frequently words match these targets.

## All ten segmentations

Every segmentation is retained below. A slash separates rune labels; adjacent Latin letters inside one label belong to a single rune.

| Candidate | Rune labels | Sum | Proposed target matched? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PROVE | P / R / O / U / E | 131 | Yes |
| WORTHIER | W / O / R / TH / I / E / R | 151 | Yes |
| WORTHIER | W / O / R / T / H / I / E / R | 228 | No |
| FIND | F / I / N / D | 151 | Yes |
| TRUTHS | T / R / U / TH / S | 131 | Yes |
| TRUTHS | T / R / U / T / H / S | 208 | No |
| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / EO / N / T / I / D / A / E | 809 | Yes |
| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / EO / N / T / I / D / AE | 746 | No |
| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / E / O / N / T / I / D / A / E | 842 | No |
| MYRMELEONTIDAE | M / Y / R / M / E / L / E / O / N / T / I / D / AE | 779 | No |

All five targets are achievable, each by one segmentation. PROVE and FIND each have only one segmentation under the declared rules. WORTHIER and TRUTHS each have two; MYRMELEONTIDAE has four.

## The 809 match requires a particular segmentation

MYRMELEONTIDAE gives 809 when EO is combined but the final A and E are separate. Combining both EO and AE gives 746. Separating both pairs gives 842; combining only the final AE gives 779. These alternatives differ because a two-letter rune's prime value is not the sum of its two separate letters' values.

A converter that always consumes the longest available label would choose EO and AE and return 746. A converter that always treats each Latin letter separately would return 842. The proposed 809 result is therefore possible within the exhaustive search, but it is not determined by the spelling alone. No evidence here selects that segmentation as the manuscript's intended representation.

## What the phrase match establishes

The matching totals for PROVE WORTHIER FIND TRUTHS are 131, 151, 151 and 131. That verifies four arithmetic assignments. It does not recover their order, grammar or intended meaning from the square. Choosing words for their fitting totals and then observing that those totals are prime is not a second independent test: the target numbers already supplied that property.

The [mixed-square guide](#/wiki/magic-squares) distinguishes LP1-05's 1033 square, LP1-16's 3301 square and the separate LP2-15 panel. This variant associates the first four targets with LP1-05 and 809 with LP1-16; it does not move the red 3299 from LP2-15 into either square. A claimed thematic relation of a word to insect imagery would require separate evidence and is not tested here.

## Reproduce and inspect

```text
python experiments/records/selected-phrase-word-sums/run.py --check
python experiments/records/selected-phrase-word-sums/check.py
```

The runner is byte-identical to the baseline runner and reads this variant's plan. Without `--check`, it prints the complete JSON report. The independent checker enumerates every cut/no-cut choice between Latin letters, rejects pieces absent from the alphabet, and verifies all retained segmentations and totals. Both commands passed in the extracted reproduction bundle. Python's standard library is sufficient; no dictionary download or hosted AI is involved.

## Limits and next variants

No alternative words, synonyms or dictionary entries were searched. No cipher was applied to the manuscript, and no null model estimates the surprise of the selected words. The finding neither proves an intended phrase nor shows that these are the only fitting words.

A broader word search must pin its vocabulary, normalization and segmentation policy, then retain all matches. A fixed longest-label policy would be a different variant. A cipher test using these candidates must specify the target pages, transform, key advancement and success criterion. The [rune-length bounds](#/wiki/prime-sums?section=length-bounds) can rule out impossible lengths before a dictionary search starts.

records.article:
# Does removing one rune type reduce LP2’s adjacent repeats?

No, under the fixed rule tested here. For each of the 29 rune types, remove **every occurrence of that type** from LP2-00–55 and recount equal adjacent runes within pages. The archived stream has **86 doublets**. Every one-type deletion leaves **92 to 109**, so none reduces the raw count. This closes a small, explicit class of null-removal suggestions; it does not test arbitrary null positions or whether deletion before a later cipher could help.

![Adjacent equal-rune counts for every fixed one-type deletion](experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/single-rune-null-doublets.svg)

## What was fixed

The inputs are the 56 archived LP2-00–55 page texts and the stored 29-rune alphabet. Headings are included. Within each page, remove non-runes as in the [published doublet census](#/wiki/doublets); never count a pair across pages. For each rune type, delete all its occurrences, leave all surviving runes in order, and count adjacent equal pairs again. The rule has exactly **29 configurations**, not a search over individual positions. The [plan](experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/plan.json) and source hashes make the corpus and comparison explicit.

| Result | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Original adjacent equal pairs | 86 of 12,901 within-page edges |
| Lowest after a one-type deletion | 92 (G, W, S or NG) |
| Highest after a one-type deletion | 109 (R) |
| Fixed-count shuffle expectation after deletion | 437.08–440.80 pairs, depending on type |

Deleting a type can destroy an existing pair of that rune, but it can also bring two formerly separated surviving runes together. For G, five old G–G pairs disappear while 11 new equal pairs form across deleted runs, giving **86 − 5 + 11 = 92**. For R, two old pairs disappear and 25 new bridges form, giving **109**. The [complete result](experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/results.json) records the removed symbols, destroyed pairs, new bridges, surviving edges, rate and reference expectation for every type. Its exact bridge accounting is checked independently.

The fixed-count shuffle expectation is calculated separately from each **retained** page’s rune frequencies. The observed-to-expected ratio stays between **0.209 and 0.248** across the 29 deletions. That comparison says the low-adjacency feature is still visible after this transformation relative to a within-page shuffle of the retained symbols. It is **not** a probability that a null model is false, and a shuffled stream is not a plaintext-language model.

## What this does and does not close

If the proposal is specifically “one rune type is padding, and deleting all of it will remove the low-doublet feature from the raw LP2 stream,” these 29 exhaustive cases do not support it. A different claim could delete only selected positions, delete several rune types, preserve word boundaries differently, or delete before applying a cipher whose alignment then changes. Those have much larger search spaces and need separate bounds and controls. A readable fragment after hand-selecting deleted positions would not be comparable with this fixed sweep.

This record measures a ciphertext statistic. It does not recover plaintext, identify a null symbol, or rule out nulls in general. The [null-removal guide](#/wiki/method-nulls) explains the larger family and the order-of-operations issue; the [doublet guide](#/wiki/doublets) defines the 86-pair baseline.

## Reproduce

From the repository root or extracted [experiment ZIP](downloads/experiments/single-rune-null-doublets.zip), using Python 3 standard library:

```text
python experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/run.py --check
python experiments/records/single-rune-null-doublets/check.py
```

The producer checks every input hash and reproduces the report and SVG. The separate checker extracts rune streams through a different parser, verifies the destroyed-pair and bridge identity for all 29 cases, and recalculates every edge count and exact fixed-count shuffle expectation. Both compare the same declared source files; neither re-reads the manuscript images.

records.article:
## Why match the number of tokens?

The [aligned-language baseline](#/experiments/parallel-languages) compares the manuscript with much longer reference texts. This control asks a narrower question: how do those reference languages behave when each sample contains exactly **2,896 tokens**, the size of the unsolved rune-token target?

Every complete reference sample is nearest to its own language profile. However, **the manuscript is farther from every language profile than any of that language's reference samples are**. English is still the nearest of the eight candidates, but nearest does not mean that its profile closely explains the manuscript. These are observed distances, not probabilities or statistical rejection thresholds.

## What is held fixed

The languages, translations, development profiles, three common representations and total-variation distance are inherited from the baseline. There is no fitted classifier or new language selection. Each evaluation translation is tokenized sentence by sentence, then divided in original order into disjoint blocks of 2,896 tokens. Every complete block is retained; the final incomplete remainder is counted and reported but not scored as an equal-size sample.

This produces seven blocks each for English and German, eight each for French, Italian, Portuguese, Spanish and Welsh, and five for Finnish. The three representations reuse the same texts. The resulting 177 profile checks are **not 177 independent trials**, and they are not pooled into a claimed general classification accuracy.

Equal token counts do not preserve identical translated passages: different languages use different numbers of words for the same content. This control addresses size. The [aligned-block variant](#/experiments/parallel-language-blocks) separately preserves sentence ranges across languages. Neither controls for the difference between translated web material and Liber Primus's style.

## Reading the distances

Each sample is compared with all eight full development profiles using length bins 1 through 15 and 16+. Total variation is half the sum of the absolute differences in bin proportions. Zero means matching distributions; larger values mean greater separation. All distances are stored as exact rational numbers, and ties would be retained rather than broken by language order.

| Language | Complete blocks per representation | Largest letter-control distance | Manuscript to letter profile |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| English | 7 | 0.0508 | 0.0831 |
| Finnish | 5 | 0.0466 | 0.4051 |
| French | 8 | 0.0514 | 0.1781 |
| German | 7 | 0.0561 | 0.1665 |
| Italian | 8 | 0.0436 | 0.2375 |
| Portuguese | 8 | 0.0426 | 0.2114 |
| Spanish | 8 | 0.0456 | 0.2230 |
| Welsh | 8 | 0.0404 | 0.1650 |

“Largest control distance” means the farthest observed sample from its own language's development profile. It is not a confidence limit. The manuscript lies beyond those observed ranges for all eight languages in all three representations, including GP-style grouping. That grouping is an orthographic sensitivity, not a validated conversion of each language into runes.

Within this corpus, all complete samples have a unique nearest profile matching their known language. The manuscript's nearest profile is English in all three representations. The report preserves every competing distance and the margin over the nearest competing language, so this statement can be checked without relying on a winner-only table.

## A Unicode exception found before scoring

The original follow-up plan assumed that all three representations would preserve token boundaries. The implementation stopped when that check failed. Lowercasing the capital dotted I in “İzmir” creates an i followed by a combining dot; the inherited raw-letter tokenizer treats the mark as a separator. Accent folding removes it, joining the word. Three source sentences are affected.

An amendment was committed after inspecting that tokenization issue and before inspecting follow-up scores. The baseline tokenizer was not silently changed. Each representation is partitioned independently, its endpoint ledger is retained, and the report states whether boundaries agree. Folded letters and GP grouping do share boundaries. The original plan remains available alongside the amendment.

## What this does not establish

The control does not identify the manuscript's language, eliminate the eight languages, or estimate a posterior probability. The sample ranges are small, adjacent blocks can share a source article, and both reference splits come from the same benchmark. The manuscript has different genre, spelling, unit and boundary uncertainties. Even its closest reference profile can therefore be a poor match for reasons other than language.

The [known-reading control](#/experiments/known-reading-languages) supplies a complementary warning: some short, established English sections rank nearest to other language profiles. The [cipher-invariants guide](#/wiki/cipher-invariants) explains which transformations preserve lengths and which change the assumptions behind this comparison.

## Reproduce and inspect

Python 3's standard library is sufficient; no API or model is involved. From the repository or extracted reproduction bundle, choose new output filenames:

```sh
python scripts/run_target_sized_languages.py --output my-language-controls.json
```
